column2: If it is in another country, badly written, lost, erased, taken, broken, cut or burnt, another document should be made.
For clearing a doubtful matter, what is written in one's own hand, with reasons, receipt, act, marks, connection, title and cause,
the entry should be written on the back of the document of what the debtor has paid; and the creditor should give a receipt marked with his own hand.
Having paid the debt, one should tear the document and have another made for purity; what has witnesses should be given with witnesses.
Balance, fire, water, poison and the sacred libation are the ordeals here for purification; in great charges these are used when the accuser is at the head.
Either may undergo it by choice, the other staking his head; even without staking the head in treason against the king or a sin.
One should not take the ploughshare under a thousand, nor the balance nor poison; in charges concerning the king's affairs the pure ones should always carry it.
For a thousand, balance and the rest; the sacred libation one may have given even for little; for fifty one should have the pure one pay; the impure becomes liable to the fine.
Having called him, bathed in his clothes and fasting at sunrise, one should have the divine ordeals done in the presence of the king and Brahmins.
The balance is for women, children, old, blind, lame, Brahmins and the sick; fire or water for a Shudra, or seven barley grains of poison.
The accused, by those learned in holding the balance, being placed on the balance, becoming equal to the counterweight, is brought down having made a mark.
Sun and Moon, wind, fire, sky, earth, water, the heart and Yama, day and night and both twilights, and Dharma know a man's conduct.

You, Balance, are the seat of truth, made of old by the gods; speak truth, auspicious one; free me from doubt.
agnipuran:253:37	If I am a sinner, mother, take me down; if pure, lift me up — one should address the balance thus.
Having marked the hands with rubbed rice, one should then place (the iron); seven pipal leaves one should wrap with thread in as many turns.
You, Fire, move within all beings as a witness; tell the truth of my merit and sin.
To him having said so, an iron lump equal, of fifty palas, fire-colored, one should place in both hands;
he should take it and walk seven circles, a hundred (steps each); a circle is to be known as sixteen fingers, so the interval.
Having released the fire, the one with rubbed rice unburnt attains purity. If the lump falls in between or in doubt he should carry it again.
You are the purifier of purifiers, Fire; purify the one to be purified; protect me with truth — thus for the accused, with the Varuna mantra.
Standing in navel-deep water, holding the thighs, one should enter the water; a swift man should fetch an arrow shot at the same time;
if he sees the immersed limb, he attains purity. "You, Poison, son of Brahma, established in truth and dharma,
protect us from this curse; by truth be nectar to me" — having said so he should eat the Himalayan poison, sarnga;
for whom it is digested without effects, one should declare purification. Having worshipped the fierce gods one should bring their bathing water;
having made him hear, he should be made to drink three handfuls of that water. For whom, until the fourteenth day, no calamity from king or fate
arises terribly, he would be pure without doubt. Truth, vehicles, weapons, cows, seeds and gold,
gods and teachers' feet, and the sacrificial and pious works done: these are declared easy oaths in slight doubt.
One who recovers property that has come in order and been taken, he should not give it to the co-heirs; nor what was gained by learning.
What was given to one by his parents is his wealth alone. For those who divide after the father, the mother too takes an equal share.
The uninitiated are to be initiated by earlier-initiated brothers, and the sisters by giving a fourth part from their own shares.
Sons of a Brahmin by caste would have four, three, two, one shares; Kshatriya's sons three, two, one; Vaishya's sons two and one.
What is seen to have been taken from each other when divided, that again they should divide in equal shares — so it is established.
A son begotten on another's field by appointment by a childless man is heir to both and a pinda-giver by dharma.
The own-born son of the dharma-wife; equal to him the appointed daughter's son; the field-born, born in the field, of the same gotra or another;
the one born hidden in the house is the secretly-born son; the maiden-born is held the maternal grandfather's son;
the one born of a woman, violated or not, again married is the son of a remarried woman; one whom mother or father would give is the given son;
one bought and sold by them is the made-son; self-made; the self-given by himself; found in the womb, the co-married-born;
one abandoned and taken up is the cast-off son. The pinda-giver and share-taker of these, in absence of the earlier, the later.
This rule was told by me for sons of the same caste. Even one born of a Shudra's slave woman by desire becomes a share-taker.
When the father is dead the brothers should make him a half-share holder; the one without brothers takes all, except for daughters of the son.
Wife, daughters, parents, brothers, their sons, gotra-kin, relatives, pupil, fellow students —
in absence of these, the later takes the wealth of the earlier; for one who has gone to heaven childless this rule is in all castes.
Heirs of forest-dwellers, ascetics and students are in order the teacher, good pupil, dharma-brother, and co-pilgrim.
A reunited one to the reunited, a uterine brother to the uterine; one should give and take a share of one born and one dead.
The reunited of another womb should not take the wealth of another womb; even unreunited, the uterine brother may take, not another.
The fallen, his son, the impotent, the lame, the mad, the dull, the blind, those with incurable disease and the like, share-less, are to be maintained;
the own-born and field-born of these are blameless and share-takers. Their sons should be well maintained as long as they are made dependent on the husband.
Childless wives of these are to be maintained if of good conduct; adulteresses and the contrary should be turned out.
What was given by father, mother, husband, brother, what was received before the fire, and the supersession gift, is declared woman's property;
what was given by kin, bride-price, and later gifts. If she dies childless, her relatives would obtain it.
The childless woman's property goes to her husband in the four marriages beginning with Brahma; if she has daughters, to the daughters; in the rest, to the father's side.
One who takes back a maiden after giving her should be fined and pay the cost with interest; if she has died, he may take what was given after settling both expenses.
In famine, in a dharma act, in disease and in obstruction, woman's property taken by the husband — he need not give it back to the woman.
To the superseded wife one should give an equal supersession-payment; one to whom no woman's property was given, if given, half is declared.
In denial of partition, partition is to be known by kinsmen, relatives, witnesses, documents, houses, fields and marriage property.
As long as the crop is destroyed, so long the field-owner gets the fruit; the herdsman is to be beaten, and the cow-owner deserves the previously stated fine.
On the road, at the village boundary, in a field — no fault exists; when done unintentionally in free grazing he deserves a thief's fine.
Great bulls, released animals, a cow that has calved and a visiting cow, whose herdsman should release them, flooded by fate or king.
As the cowherd was given the animals, so should he return them in the evening; for those dead or lost through negligence he should pay; he has been paid wages.
On damage by the herdsman's fault, a fine is ordained for the herdsman: twelve and a half panas and the owner's goods.
Cow-pasture by village wish or by the king's authority; a twice-born may take grass, fuel and flowers everywhere as his own.
A hundred bows is the circumference between village and field; two hundred for a market-town; four hundred for a city.
One may obtain what is his own sold by another; the buyer's fault when not made known; the thief who sells secretly at low price, or at the wrong time.
Having found what was lost or taken, one should have the thief seized; or having taken it, if the place and time have passed, one should himself hand it over;
by sight of the seller there is purity; the owner (gets) the thing, the king the fine; the buyer gets the price from the seller there.
What is lost is to be established by title and possession, otherwise not; for him the fine is five-bound to the king, if not established.
One who gets from another's hand goods that were taken or lost, without informing the king, is fined — he pays six panas;
what was lost and taken is recovered by toll-keepers or station guards; before a year the owner gets it; after that the king.
For a one-hoofed animal one should give four panas; five for a man; two each for buffalo, camel, cow; a quarter each for sheep and goat.
One should give without conflict with one's family, except wife and sons. When there is lineage, not all property should be given, nor what is promised to another;
acceptance should be open, especially for immovables. What is to be given and what is promised, having given one should not take back.
Waiting periods: ten, one, five, seven days, a month, three days, half a month — for seeds, iron, carriage, jewels, women, milch animals, men.
In fire gold is not lost; in silver two palas per hundred; eight in tin and lead; fifteen in copper and iron;
wool and cotton ten palas increase per hundred; in medium five palas to be known; in fine three palas is held;
in worked and hair-bound goods a thirtieth part is held loss; no loss nor increase in silk and bark-cloth.
